$comment: ★★ A COMMON BESIDE A WEAK DEFINITION OF ITS NAME ON MACH-O: THE DEFINITION REPLACES THE COMMON (P69 send-back 5, review-xa4 MINOR 4; D-LK-COMMON-OUTRANKED-A-WEAK-DEFINITION-IN-EVERY-FORMAT) -- the Mach-O documents' `commonYieldsTo: anyDefinition`, on the reference compiler's own objects. The two objects named to the link are Apple clang's builds of `int dss_tentative; int dss_read_tentative(void) { return dss_tentative; }` under `-fcommon` (`(common) (alignment 2^2) external _dss_tentative`) and of `__attribute__((weak)) int dss_tentative = 5;` (`(__DATA,__data) weak external _dss_tentative`). ✔MEASURED 2026-10-08 (the same main.c built by Apple clang 21.0.0, ld-1267; arm64 and x86_64): in both object orders the weak definition replaces the common and the program reads 5, exit 42; the common object alone reads 0, exit 37. GNU ld answers the opposite on ELF and for MinGW's spelling on PE -- the common outranks a weak definition, 0 (`examples/c/common_beside_a_weak_definition_elf`, `examples/c/common_beside_a_weak_definition_pe_mingw`) -- which is why the answer is a key of the format document rather than a rule of the link. main.c is DSS's; the 37 it adds keeps either answer apart from the exit code of a program that did nothing -- a link that kept the common would exit 37. The `release` arm pins that optimizing the DSS half changes nothing about which of the two the program reads.
